title: Magnetic Imaging with High Spatial Resolution Using a Single Niobium-Nitride-Based Three-Dimensional Nanobridge Junction
authors: Yinping Pan, Yue Wang, Xinxin Fan, Xu Liu, Shirui Liu, Xiaoyu Liu, Ling Wu, Lu Zhang, Wei Peng, Jie Ren, Jiamin Xiong, Hao Li, Lixing You, Zhen Wang, Lei Chen
abstract: The nanobridge junctions (NBJs) allow the miniaturization of the Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) and improve the spatial resolution of scanning SQUID microscopy. However, the SQUID loop diameter imposed a fundamental limit on the resolution. In this work, we proposed a single niobium-nitride-based three-dimensional nanobridge junction (NbN-3D-NBJ) alternative to the nanoSQUID for high-resolution magnetic imaging. The critical current of an NbN-3D-NBJ showed an nearly monotonic dependence on the external magnetic field, enabling nanoscale mapping of the magnetic field distribution by measuring the junction's critical current with an intrinsic noise level of 100 nT/Hz^1/2. Using a NbN-3D-NBJ probe, we successfully imaged an Abrikosov vortex in a niobium film with a minimal full width at half maxima (FWHM) of 530 nm, constrained by the distance from the junction to the probe tip edge. Furthermore, we resolved 80 nm spacings between the superconducting nanowires utilizing a second probe with an optimized junction-to-tip distance. Thus, the single 3D NbN NBJ probe has been demonstrated as an effective approach for magnetic imaging with ultra-high spatial resolution.
summary: The authors developed and utilized a novel Niobium-Nitride-Based Three-Dimensional Nanobridge Junction (NbN-3D-NBJ) probe to overcome resolution limits in magnetic imaging. By measuring the junction's critical current while scanning, they successfully imaged Abrikosov vortices and resolved spacings as small as 80 nm. This demonstrates the probe's potential for ultra-high-resolution magnetic characterization in condensed matter systems.
main_problem: The primary goal is to overcome the fundamental spatial resolution limits of conventional SQUID-based magnetic imaging to achieve nanoscale mapping of magnetic fields.
main_result: The proposed single Niobium-Nitride-Based Three-Dimensional Nanobridge Junction (NbN-3D-NBJ) probe successfully demonstrated ultra-high spatial resolution, achieving a minimum Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of 530 nm and resolving 80 nm spacings.
method: Magnetic field mapping is performed by measuring the critical current ($I_c$) of the NbN-3D-NBJ as it scans over the sample surface, with the resolution being limited by the junction-to-tip distance.
model_or_system: The system utilizes a 3D nanobridge junction fabricated from Niobium-Nitride (NbN) as a highly sensitive magnetic sensor. This probe is used to image magnetic features like Abrikosov vortices in superconducting films.
key_observables: Critical current ($I_c$) dependence on external magnetic field ($B_z$), Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of vortex images, and magnetic noise level ($100 	ext{ nT}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$).
important_parameters: Junction-to-tip distance ($r$), superconducting film material (Niobium), and the ability to resolve spacings down to 80 nm.
main_assumptions: The current spatial resolution is primarily limited by the physical distance between the junction and the sample tip, rather than the intrinsic properties of the junction itself.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images of the probe, cross-sections, and contour maps illustrating the magnetic field dependence of the junction voltage ($V_{	ext{NBJ}}$) and the spatial mapping of vortices and nanowire patterns.
paper_structure: The paper details the fabrication and setup of the 3D NbN-NBJ probe, presents measurements of its magnetic response, and then applies it to image magnetic vortices and resolve nanoscale superconducting nanowire spacings.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant experimental advancement in nanoscale magnetometry, providing a practical, high-resolution tool for studying superconducting phenomena, which is relevant to understanding quantum electrodynamics in condensed matter systems.
